title: Gluten Teriyaki with Rice

yield.description: deeply savory seitan pieces in glossy teriyaki-style sauce, served with rice

source_context.notes: Based on the gluten teriyaki dinner using vital wheat gluten, rice, soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, and a salty sauce adjustment.

ingredients.name: vital wheat gluten
ingredients.notes: Add a little more if the dough feels too loose or sticky.

ingredients.name: garlic salt
ingredients.notes: Use less soy sauce if garlic salt is already salty.

ingredients.name: soy sauce
ingredients.notes: Dial down if using garlic salt or a salty sauce.

ingredients.name: sugar
ingredients.notes: Use more if the sauce needs balancing after tasting.

ingredients.name: cornstarch
ingredients.notes: Use only if you want a thicker, glossier sauce.

ingredients.name: rice
ingredients.notes: Use enough for 3 people. Mixing a small amount of calrose with long-grain rice is acceptable.

ingredients.name: water
ingredients.notes: Use the appropriate amount for your rice type and cooking method.

steps.title: Cook the rice
steps.action: Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear, then cook using your normal stovetop or rice-cooker method.
targets: ready before the seitan is sauced
notes: Start the rice first so the teriyaki seitan can be served immediately after saucing.

steps.title: Mix the dry seitan ingredients
steps.action: Combine vital wheat gluten, nutritional yeast, garlic salt, and black pepper in a mixing bowl.
risk_points: Uneven seasoning can create salty pockets in the dough.

steps.title: Form the seitan dough
steps.action: Add water and soy sauce to the dry ingredients. Mix until a cohesive dough forms, then knead briefly.
risk_points: Too much kneading can make the seitan rubbery.
Too much liquid can make the dough sticky and hard to shape.
notes: If the dough is too sticky, add vital wheat gluten 1 tbsp at a time until manageable.

steps.title: Shape the seitan
steps.action: Shape the dough into a compact slab or several thick pieces suitable for steaming.

steps.title: Steam the seitan
steps.action: Steam the shaped seitan until firm and cooked through.
risk_points: Under-steamed seitan can remain gummy inside.

steps.title: Rest and cut
steps.action: Let the steamed seitan rest briefly, then cut or tear it into bite-size pieces.
notes: Torn edges brown better than perfectly smooth cuts.

steps.title: Mix the teriyaki sauce
steps.action: Combine soy sauce, water, sugar, vinegar, ginger, and garlic. If using cornstarch, mix it separately with 1 tbsp water to form a slurry.
notes: Keep the cornstarch slurry separate until the sauce is hot.

steps.title: Sear the seitan
steps.action: Heat neutral oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add seitan pieces and brown on multiple sides.
risk_points: Crowding the pan causes steaming instead of browning.
Adding sauce too early prevents crust formation.

steps.title: Glaze with sauce
steps.action: Lower heat to medium, add the teriyaki sauce, and toss the seitan until coated. Add cornstarch slurry if using, then simmer briefly until glossy.
risk_points: Reducing too long can make the sauce overly salty.
Too much cornstarch can make the glaze pasty.

steps.title: Serve
steps.action: Serve the glazed seitan over rice immediately.

technique_notes.note: Vital wheat gluten hydrates quickly and becomes elastic. Knead only enough to form structure; excessive kneading pushes the texture toward rubbery.
Steaming sets the gluten network before browning. Searing raw seitan dough directly can leave the interior gummy.
The seitan should be relatively dry on the surface before searing. Browning creates the savory base that keeps the final dish from tasting like plain gluten in sauce.
Soy sauce, garlic salt, and reduced sauce can compound quickly. If using garlic salt, reduce soy sauce in the dough or sauce.
If the sauce is too salty, vinegar and sugar can rebalance perception, but dilution is the cleanest correction when salt is excessive.

substitutes.name: garlic powder plus salt
substitutes.ratio: use 0.25 tsp garlic powder plus salt to taste

substitutes.name: fresh garlic
substitutes.ratio: 1 small clove per 0.5 tsp garlic salt
substitutes.effect: sharper garlic flavor and less integrated seasoning

substitutes.name: sesame oil
substitutes.ratio: use a small amount mixed with neutral oil
substitutes.effect: stronger toasted aroma; can dominate if used alone

adjustments.fix: Add vital wheat gluten 1 tbsp at a time until the dough is cohesive and shapeable.
Serve with more plain rice and increase vinegar and sugar slightly in the sauce. For future batches, reduce soy sauce or garlic salt.
Dilute with water, then rebalance with sugar and vinegar.
Simmer briefly or add a small cornstarch slurry.
Add water 1 tbsp at a time and toss over low heat until loosened.
Dry the pieces better, increase heat slightly, avoid crowding the pan, and do not add sauce until browning is established.

storage.reheat: Reheat gently in a skillet or microwave with a splash of water to loosen the glaze.

nutrition_notes: Salt level depends heavily on soy sauce and garlic salt.
Serve with rice or vegetables to balance the concentrated gluten and sauce.
